title: Using Our 4 IL Slots and Stashing in a Daily League
brief: When is an injured or backup player worth holding in our daily league with 2 bench and 4 IL slots, and when should we cut him for a streamer? It must explain the new Yahoo IL rules (out players go straight to IL, questionable ones do not) and why most stash advice is for other formats.
summary: Our league uses daily lineups, has only 2 bench spots and no games cap, so most stash advice does not apply to us. Use the 4 IL slots for players already tagged out. Cut any stash as soon as you need the slot, because a streaming spot is worth about the 100th-ranked player. Do not draft or hold healthy backups for injury upside. Add them on waivers once the starter is ruled out.

sections.heading: Why most stash advice is not for us

paragraphs.text: Most experts say stashing works in certain formats: best ball, draft-only, weekly lock, roto, deep-bench, games-cap and low-transaction leagues. Our league is none of these. We set lineups daily, we have only 2 bench spots, there is no games cap, and we can make up to 6 acquisitions per week.
Several experts say it plainly. Do not stash in standard daily leagues with small benches. Daily changes and short benches make stashing risky. Deep benches and games limits reward speculation.

The cost is streaming. In a standard format, a roster spot that plays two games a week hurts your streaming. Players who play few games and minutes waste a slot in leagues where you must use every slot. A streaming spot is worth about as much as the 100th-ranked player. Every day you hold a player who does not play, you lose that production.

So when you read stash advice, check the format first. If it says weekly, roto, deep bench or games cap, discount it for our league. If it mentions 16 teams, discount it too. In 16-team leagues the advice is to draft promising rookies, but we have 12 teams and 144 drafted players.

Yahoo removed IL+. A player tagged out or injured can now go on IL right away. A player tagged questionable, doubtful or probable cannot. In our league, a questionable player has to sit in an active spot or in one of our 2 bench spots.
Under the old rules, managers parked questionable players on IL. That trick gave only a small edge. Keeping the spot open for streaming gave more flexibility. Losing the trick costs us little.

Our league has 4 IL slots. One expert says that leagues without IL+ should turn the old IL+ spots into regular IL spots, not bench spots, so the total number of injury spots stays the same. That gives us real room for players who are ruled out. It does not give us room for healthy backups or questionable players.

How much this helps depends on how fast Yahoo changes a player's status to out. Until the tag says out, the player takes up a normal roster spot. Check the status every day before you set your lineup. Move a player to IL as soon as he is tagged out.

sections.heading: When to hold an injured player and when to cut him

paragraphs.text: Price matters. A late injured player costs little because the gap between a pick around 110 and your next pick is small. Stashing one at pick 60 costs much more. In our 144-player auction, that means an injured player is only worth a minimum bid at the end of the draft. Do not spend mid-auction money on one.

An injured star is fine as a last-round stash in an IL spot. Keep him there only while you have an empty IL slot. Once all 4 IL slots are full and you need one, drop him for a waiver player. Do not give up streaming to hold him.

One expert gives a time frame for long-term injuries. Use the IL slot if you have it, but cut the player once you need the spot after the first two weeks. In our league, the first weeks after the 2026-10-18 draft are when you can still afford a free IL slot.

Your record matters too. The better your team is doing, the longer you can hold struggling or injured players. If you are losing weekly matchups, the streaming spot is worth more to you than the stash.

A healthy backup cannot go on IL, so he uses one of our 2 bench spots. Experts say backups who would only matter if the starter got hurt are worth drafting in games-cap, limited-transaction, roto and weekly-lock leagues. They are harder to justify in daily leagues where you use your bench all the time.

A backup center is not worth a roster spot until the starter in front of him is out. Drafting a backup center and waiting for a trade is usually a waste, especially if he does not produce well per minute. A deep bench player who needs several teammates hurt is not a must-draft.

If you do watch a backup, choose the right type. The best one is a clear one-for-one backup who would start and play 30-plus minutes if the starter got hurt. In our league, do not draft him. Keep him on a watch list. Bid FAB on him the day the starter is ruled out. A backup big can also be streamed for blocks.

The experts split on injured players. One view says do not draft or stash a long-term injured player at all, and only keep one in an empty injured slot. The other view says an injured star is fine as a last-round pick to stash on IL, because a late pick costs little. Both sides agree on the exit: drop him once you need the slot.

They also split on injury-prone players. One expert says players like Kristaps Porzingis are hard to use in daily leagues with small benches. Another is not sure injury-prone players should drop further, because the IL change lets them go on IL as soon as they are ruled out. Moving injury-prone players up the board is advice for games-cap leagues, which we are not. For us, the deciding question is how fast Yahoo tags the player out. A player who keeps showing up as questionable will block a bench spot.
